title: Calcium: The Messenger Kept at Arm's Length

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: How can free cytosolic calcium control different responses in the same cell without switching on everything at once?
cards.back: Cells give meaning to calcium by controlling where and when free calcium rises: local domains, whole-cell waves and spike frequency let one ion reach different readers.
cards.quote: Cells give calcium meaning by controlling where and when free calcium rises.

cards.front: A resting cell holds free cytosolic calcium near {{c1::100 nanomolar}}, while outside calcium is 1 to 2 millimolar.
cards.quote: A resting cell holds it near 100 nanomolar; outside, calcium is 1 to 2 millimolar, ten to twenty thousand times higher.
cards.section: Build the rise: gradient, channels and removal

cards.front: Why can a cell not end a calcium signal by destroying calcium, as it can end a cAMP signal by breaking the molecule down? How does it end the signal instead?
cards.back: Calcium is an element that no enzyme can make or destroy. The signal ends by moving calcium out of the free cytosolic pool, using pumps, exchangers and buffers.
cards.quote: calcium is an element that no enzyme can make or destroy, so it signals only by being moved
cards.section: Build the rise: gradient, channels and removal

cards.front: Why does opening a calcium channel raise bulk cytosolic calcium so quickly and so strongly?
cards.back: The resting level is so low that a modest number of ions raises bulk calcium about tenfold, to roughly 1 micromolar, and much higher beside the pore.
cards.why: Ions begin crossing within milliseconds of a channel opening.
cards.quote: Because the resting level is so low, a modest number of ions raises bulk cytosolic calcium about tenfold, to roughly 1 micromolar
cards.section: Build the rise: gradient, channels and removal

cards.front: What is the free calcium concentration inside the endoplasmic reticulum?
cards.back: Several hundred micromolar.
cards.quote: In the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), the cell's folded internal calcium store, free calcium is several hundred micromolar
cards.section: Build the rise: gradient, channels and removal

cards.front: Which channels on the ER release stored calcium into the cytosol, and is each an 'on' or an 'off' mechanism?
cards.back: The IP3 receptor and the ryanodine receptor. Both are 'on' mechanisms.
cards.quote: A signal may first make another messenger, such as IP3 from the previous lesson, which opens its receptor channel on the ER.
cards.section: Build the rise: gradient, channels and removal

cards.front: What does the SERCA pump do, and how many calcium ions does it move per ATP?
cards.back: It moves calcium into the ER store, 2 calcium ions per ATP. It is an 'off' mechanism for the cytosolic signal.
cards.quote: SERCA moves 2 calcium ions into the store per ATP
cards.section: Build the rise: gradient, channels and removal

cards.front: How do the plasma-membrane PMCA and the sodium/calcium exchanger each remove calcium from the cytosol?
cards.back: PMCA expels 1 calcium ion per ATP. The exchanger uses the sodium gradient, trading 3 sodium ions in for 1 calcium ion out.
cards.quote: the sodium/calcium exchanger uses the sodium gradient, trading 3 sodium ions in for 1 calcium ion out
cards.section: Build the rise: gradient, channels and removal

cards.front: Why does a buffer such as parvalbumin count as part of the 'off' machinery?
cards.back: It binds calcium and removes it from the free pool, so the free level falls without any enzyme destroying calcium.
cards.quote: Buffers such as parvalbumin bind calcium and remove it from the free pool
cards.section: Build the rise: gradient, channels and removal

cards.front: Sealed sarcoplasmic reticulum vesicles are in 1.0 mL of buffer with 50 micromolar calcium. After ATP is added, the buffer calcium falls to 10 micromolar while 20 nanomoles of ATP are split. How many calcium ions are taken up per ATP?
cards.back: Calcium lost: 40 micromolar x 1.0 mL = 40 nanomoles. 40 / 20 = 2.0 calcium ions per ATP, matching SERCA.
cards.quote: the Heidelberg measurements put the cost at about two calcium ions per ATP split: relaxed muscle spends ATP to stay relaxed.
cards.section: Build the rise: gradient, channels and removal

cards.front: Outside calcium is 1 millimolar and resting cytosolic calcium is 100 nanomolar. By what factor does the outside-to-inside ratio change when cytosolic calcium rises tenfold to 1 micromolar?
cards.back: Resting ratio: 1 mM / 100 nM = 10,000. After the rise: 1 mM / 1 micromolar = 1,000. The ratio falls tenfold, though a steep gradient remains.
cards.quote: A resting cell holds it near 100 nanomolar; outside, calcium is 1 to 2 millimolar, ten to twenty thousand times higher.
cards.section: Build the rise: gradient, channels and removal

cards.front: A cell in calcium-free fluid receives two identical signals that open IP3 receptors. Calcium that leaves the cell between them cannot be replaced. How should the second cytosolic rise compare with the first?
cards.back: It should be smaller. SERCA can refill the ER only partly, because calcium pumped out of the cell was not replaced from outside.
cards.quote: Predict 1. A cell in calcium-free fluid receives two identical signals that open IP3 receptors.
cards.section: Build the rise: gradient, channels and removal

cards.front: A drug inhibits PMCA in a cell, and plasma-membrane channels then open briefly. Should cytosolic calcium stay high indefinitely?
cards.back: It should fall more slowly than normal but not stay high indefinitely. SERCA, the exchanger and buffers still remove calcium. The rule: several 'off' mechanisms act together.
cards.quote: PMCA expels 1 calcium ion per ATP
cards.section: Build the rise: gradient, channels and removal

cards.front: What is store-operated entry?
cards.back: Depletion of the ER calcium store is itself an instruction to open plasma-membrane channels, so calcium enters from outside.
cards.quote: proposed in 1986 that depletion is itself an instruction to open plasma-membrane channels: store-operated entry
cards.section: An empty store asks for a refill

cards.front: How do STIM1 and Orai1 work together when the ER calcium falls?
cards.back: STIM1, an ER membrane protein, senses low luminal calcium, clusters beneath the plasma membrane and opens Orai1, which admits calcium.
cards.quote: When luminal calcium falls, STIM1 clusters beneath the plasma membrane and opens Orai1.
cards.section: An empty store asks for a refill

cards.front: A drug empties the ER while no calcium is outside, then calcium is restored outside. What happens in a cell lacking STIM1?
cards.back: The sharp store-operated rise should be largely missing. Orai1 cannot sense ER calcium by itself, and STIM1 is the main store sensor.
cards.quote: A drug empties the ER while no calcium is outside. Calcium is then restored outside.
cards.section: An empty store asks for a refill

cards.front: In a cell that has STIM1 but lacks Orai1, the ER is emptied and calcium is restored outside. Predict the cytosolic response.
cards.back: The sharp rise should be largely missing. STIM1 can sense the empty store, but Orai1 is the channel that admits calcium to the cytosol.
cards.quote: Orai1 admits calcium to the cytosol; SERCA can then pump some into the ER.
cards.section: An empty store asks for a refill

cards.front: A cell lacking STIM1 in normal outside calcium receives repeated identical IP3 signals. Predict how successive rises change, and why.
cards.back: Rises may shrink over repeats if no other entry route refills the ER: without STIM1, store depletion does not open entry, so SERCA refills the ER only with calcium already inside while pumps and exchangers expel some. The lesson gives this only for a store that never refills, which supports only a limited release.
cards.quote: A store that never refills supports only a limited release.
cards.section: An empty store asks for a refill

cards.front: How can a protein bind calcium at about 1 micromolar but stay mostly empty at 100 nanomolar?
cards.back: It forms an oxygen-lined pocket suited to calcium's double positive charge. Its affinity (Kd) puts filling near a micromolar.
cards.quote: A protein can therefore make an oxygen-lined pocket that is mostly empty at 100 nanomolar and fills around a micromolar
cards.section: How a protein reads the rise

cards.front: In an EF hand, calcium sits in a twelve-residue {{c1::loop}} between helices E and F.
cards.quote: calcium sits in a twelve-residue loop between helices E and F.
cards.section: How a protein reads the rise

cards.front: Which side chains supply the oxygens that coordinate calcium in an EF-hand loop?
cards.back: Aspartate and glutamate.
cards.quote: Aspartate and glutamate side chains supply oxygens around it.
cards.section: How a protein reads the rise

cards.front: Two proteins bind the same amount of calcium. Only one exposes a target-binding surface. Which is a sensor, and which could be only a buffer?
cards.back: The one that exposes a surface is a sensor, because binding changes what it can do. The other may still act as a buffer, but binding alone sends no instruction.
cards.quote: The one that exposes a surface is a sensor: binding changes what it can do.
cards.section: How a protein reads the rise

cards.front: What does calcium binding do to calmodulin?
cards.back: It exposes a hydrophobic patch on each lobe. With many targets the lobes close around a target helix; other targets use one lobe or separate sites. This is a change of shape.
cards.quote: Calcium exposes a hydrophobic, water-avoiding patch on each lobe.
cards.section: How a protein reads the rise

cards.front: How many EF hands does calmodulin have, and how are they arranged?
cards.back: Four, two in each lobe, joined by a flexible linker. The protein has 148 amino acids.
cards.quote: It has 148 amino acids and four EF hands, two in each lobe, joined by a flexible linker.
cards.section: How a protein reads the rise

cards.front: Why can one calmodulin molecule serve many different targets?
cards.back: Calmodulin has no catalytic activity of its own, and each target carries its own calmodulin-binding site.
cards.quote: Calmodulin has no catalytic activity, so one molecule can serve many targets: each target carries its own calmodulin-binding site.
cards.section: How a protein reads the rise

cards.front: How does calcium-loaded calmodulin switch on CaM kinase II (CaMKII)?
cards.back: At rest a segment blocks the active site. Calmodulin grips that segment and pulls it clear, so the kinase can phosphorylate substrates.
cards.quote: a segment blocks the active site at rest. Calcium-loaded calmodulin grips that segment and pulls it clear
cards.section: How a protein reads the rise

cards.front: A calmodulin mutant cannot bind calcium. Predict CaMKII activity in a cell expressing only this calmodulin when cytosolic calcium rises.
cards.back: CaMKII should stay off. Without calcium, calmodulin does not expose its hydrophobic patches or grip the blocking segment, so a calcium rise is not turned into a phosphate on a protein.
cards.quote: letting the kinase phosphorylate substrates. A rise in an ion has become a phosphate on a protein
cards.section: How a protein reads the rise

cards.front: In heart muscle, a local release through ryanodine receptors is a {{c1::spark}}.
cards.quote: In heart muscle, a local release through ryanodine receptors is a spark.
cards.section: Where and how often: the evidence and its limits

cards.front: How does a calcium wave cross an egg or a liver cell?
cards.back: Release from one cluster stimulates the release channels of the next, by positive feedback, so the rise travels across the cell.
cards.quote: calcium from one cluster stimulates the release channels of the next, by positive feedback, and a wave crosses the cell.
cards.section: Where and how often: the evidence and its limits

cards.front: A fast calcium buffer is added and the whole-cell calcium peak falls sharply. Should a sensor anchored beside an open channel lose its response just as sharply?
cards.back: Probably not. It sits where calcium is highest, before the buffer binds much, while the whole-cell average reflects calcium that has spread. The result depends on buffer concentration and kinetics.
cards.quote: It sits where calcium is highest, before the buffer can bind much of it
cards.section: Where and how often: the evidence and its limits

cards.front: In single rat liver cells with a light-emitting calcium reporter, more hormone was applied. What did the calcium record show about how dose is encoded?
cards.back: More hormone produced more frequent calcium spikes. The dose was written in frequency, not in a higher calcium level.
cards.quote: More hormone produced more frequent calcium spikes: the dose was written in frequency, not in a higher calcium level.
cards.section: Where and how often: the evidence and its limits

cards.front: What must a molecule be able to do to decode calcium spike frequency?
cards.back: Keep some activity from one spike to the next. Without memory, each spike would be read alone.
cards.quote: To respond to frequency, a reader must keep some activity from one spike to the next.
cards.section: Where and how often: the evidence and its limits

cards.front: How can CaMKII act as a counter of calcium pulses?
cards.back: In its hub of subunits, when two neighbours hold calmodulin together, one can phosphorylate the other, so activity can persist after calcium falls.
cards.quote: when two neighbours hold calmodulin together, one can phosphorylate the other, and activity can persist after calcium falls.
cards.section: Where and how often: the evidence and its limits

cards.front: Purified CaMKII gets 100 identical 200 ms pulses of calcium-calmodulin, once per second in one run and four times per second in another. Persistent activity is 5% versus 60%. What is the total time in calcium, and what do the data show?
cards.back: Total time is 100 x 0.2 s = 20 s in both runs. Only the interval differs, so the enzyme responds to pulse frequency, not summed calcium.
cards.quote: In 1998 De Koninck and Schulman showed with purified enzyme that lasting activity depends on pulse frequency.
cards.section: Where and how often: the evidence and its limits

cards.front: What does aequorin do when it binds calcium?
cards.back: It emits blue light, so injected into a cell it reports calcium rises as flashes.
cards.quote: emits blue light when it binds calcium
cards.section: Seeing calcium without confusing the signal

cards.front: Why is a two-wavelength ratio dye such as fura-2 a good calcium reporter?
cards.back: Its best excitation wavelength shifts on calcium binding. The ratio depends little on dye loading and can be calibrated to concentration.
cards.quote: The ratio at two wavelengths depends little on dye loading and can be calibrated to concentration.
cards.section: Seeing calcium without confusing the signal

cards.front: Design a one-chain protein that reports calcium by light, using calmodulin. Name its four parts and explain how the output changes.
cards.back: Chain: cyan fluorescent protein, calmodulin, calmodulin-binding peptide, yellow fluorescent protein. Calcium makes calmodulin grip the peptide, bringing the ends within nanometres, so FRET raises the yellow-to-cyan ratio.
cards.quote: When calcium rises, calmodulin grips its peptide and brings the ends within a few nanometres.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A twin calcium sensor has the glutamate at the end of each EF-hand loop changed to glutamine. What does it control for, and what can it not show?
cards.back: It shows the response requires calcium binding, ruling out pH or bleaching. It cannot show where the calcium came from.
cards.quote: The twin shows that the response requires calcium binding, but not where the calcium came from.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How is a calcium sensor calibrated inside cells?
cards.back: An ionophore lets calcium in to give the maximum ratio; a chelator grips calcium to give the minimum.
cards.quote: an ionophore, which carries calcium across membranes, gives the maximum ratio in high calcium, and a chelator, which grips calcium tightly, gives the minimum.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A cell expresses a very high amount of a calmodulin-based calcium reporter. Predict how this affects the calcium signal it reports.
cards.back: The reporter is itself a calcium buffer, so it dampens the rise it measures. Use as little as can be read.
cards.quote: The reporter is itself a calcium buffer, so use as little as can be read.
cards.section: Design problem
